initial_assessment: 34-year-old man, performance status 2, with one week of headache and vomiting and no reported comorbidities. MRI describes a well-circumscribed, lobulated extra-axial/cortically based left frontal mass (about 4.2 × 3.5 × 3.0 cm) and a separate 5 mm intensely enhancing posterior pial nodule at C6, with normal cervical cord caliber. Stereotactic biopsy is reported only as suggestive of an intracranial mesenchymal tumor with spinal drop metastasis. That phrasing is not a final diagnosis: histologic type, grade, and molecular class are unestablished, and no molecular result is available to define a treatable entity. The C6 nodule is concerning but unproven as drop metastasis. Symptoms may reflect raised intracranial pressure, but mass effect, hydrocephalus, seizures, and focal deficits are not documented. Disease-directed therapy is not justified on this record.
diagnostic_confirmation_and_staging: Immediate priority is specialist neuropathology review of the existing biopsy and an explicit statement of tissue adequacy. If material cannot support histology plus molecular studies, further sampling should be considered only after neurosurgical assessment of safety and resectability, not as an automatic next step. Pathology that would change management, and that is not yet available, includes architecture, mitotic rate, necrosis, and an immunohistochemical panel able to separate a true mesenchymal neoplasm from meningioma, metastasis, glioma, lymphoma, and inflammatory mimics. Molecular results that would likewise change the later plan, none of which are in hand, include nuclear STAT6 or NAB2::STAT6 (solitary fibrous tumor and its grade), methylation class, FET::CREB or other sarcoma-defining fusions (EWSR1/FUS, CIC, BCOR), DICER1 or other defining alterations, and—if lineage is revised—glioma markers such as IDH, 1p/19q, MGMT, or H3, or tumor-of-origin markers for metastasis. Confirmation of entity and grade would determine whether any later discussion of resection extent, focal radiotherapy, craniospinal treatment, systemic therapy, or genetics referral is even relevant; those choices cannot be made now. Safe staging is neuroradiology review of the brain and full spine MRI, including edema, mass effect, midline shift, hydrocephalus, bone or dural involvement, and whether thoracic, lumbar, and sacral levels were actually imaged, plus correlation of the C6 nodule before it is accepted as dissemination. Extracranial sarcoma should be excluded with body staging before the tumor is treated as a primary CNS lesion with drop metastasis. CSF cytology is not documented and should not be obtained until herniation risk is reviewed.
immediate_management_plan: Defer all disease-directed chemotherapy and definitive radiotherapy, including any craniospinal plan, until diagnosis, grade, extent, and resectability are established. Immediate care is symptom control, diagnostic confirmation, safe staging, and multidisciplinary review. Assess urgently for declining consciousness, papilledema, or focal deficit; treat headache and vomiting with analgesia and antiemetics. Use corticosteroids only if symptomatic edema or mass effect is confirmed, and avoid empiric steroids if further diagnostic tissue may still be required and lymphoma remains possible on review. Clarify seizure history rather than starting antitumor therapy. Convene neurosurgery, neuroradiology, neuropathology, and neuro-oncology to decide whether ancillary studies on the current biopsy are sufficient or whether maximal safe resection or repeat biopsy is the safer way to obtain a definitive diagnosis. Do not treat the unconfirmed C6 nodule as proven dissemination and do not select a drug, radiotherapy dose, or treatment volume at this visit.
